question.text:
The second-order differential equation

\[ y'' - 3y' + 7y= 0 \]

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = f(t) \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t)$ and $x_2(t) = y'(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1 &= y \\[5pt] x_2 & = y' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1' &= y' \\[5pt] x_2' & = y'' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = y''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain \[ y'' = 3y' - 7y. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = 3x_2 - 7x_1. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = -7x_1 + 3x_2 \end{cases} \]

Finally, $f(t) = -7x_1 + 3x_2.$

question.text:
The third-order differential equation

\[ y''' - t^{-3/2} y' - t^{-1} y= 0 \]

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3 \\[5pt] x_3' = f(t) \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t),$ and $x_3(t) = y''(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1 &= y \\[5pt] x_2 & = y'\\[5pt] x_3 & = y'' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1' = y' \\[5pt] x_2' = y''\\[5pt] x_3' = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = t^{-3/2} y' + t^{-1} y. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = t^{-3/2} x_2 + t^{-1} x_1. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3 \\[5pt] x_3' = t^{-1} x_1 + t^{-3/2} x_2 \end{cases} \]

Finally, $f(t) = t^{-1} x_1 + t^{-3/2} x_2.$

question.text:
The second-order initial value problem \[ y'' - 10y' + 25\sin{t}\,y= 0 , \quad y(0)= -1, \quad y'(0)= 2 \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(0)= p \\[0.15cm] x_2' = f(t), \quad & x_2(0)= q \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) &= y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'. \end{align}

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

\begin{align} y(0) &= x_1(0) = -1 \\[5pt] y'(0) & = x_2(0) = 2 \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) &= y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y'' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = y''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain

\[ y'' = 10y' - 25\sin{t}\,y. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = 10x_2 - 25\sin{t}\,x_1. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(0)= -1 \\[5pt] x_2' = - 25\sin{t}\,x_1+10x_2, \quad& x_2(0)= 2 \end{cases} \]

Finally, $p=-1, q=2, f(t) = -25\sin{t}\,x_1 + 10x_2,$ and

\begin{align*} (p-q)\cdot f(t) &= (-1-2)(-25\sin{t}\,x_1 + 10x_2) \\[5pt] &= -3(-5)(5\sin{t}\,x_1 - 2x_2)\\[5pt] & = 15(5\sin{t}\,x_1 - 2x_2). \end{align*}

question.text:
The second-order initial value problem \[ y'' - 3y' + 2y= 0 , \quad y(1)= 2, \quad y'(1)= 3 \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(1)= p \\[0.15cm] x_2' = f(t), \quad & x_2(1)= q \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) &= y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'. \end{align}

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

\begin{align} y(1) &= x_1(1) = 2 \\[5pt] y'(1) & = x_2(1) = 3 \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) &= y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y'' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = y''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain

\[ y'' = 3y' - 2y. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = 3x_2 - 2x_1. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(1)= 2 \\[5pt] x_2' = - 2x_1+3x_2, \quad& x_2(1)= 3 \end{cases} \]

Finally, $p=2, q=3, f(t) = - 2x_1+3x_2,$ and

\begin{align*} (p-q)\cdot f(t) &= (2-3)f(t) \\[5pt] &= -f(t) \\[5pt] &= 2x_1-3x_2. \end{align*}

question.text:
The third-order initial value problem \[ y''' + 3y' = 0 , \quad y(2)= -1, \quad y'(2)= 1, \quad y''(2)= 2 \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(2)= p \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3, \quad& x_2(2)= q \\[5pt] x_3' = f(t), \quad & x_3(2)= r \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t),$ $x_3(t) = y''(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate $(p+q-r)\cdot f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) &= y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'\\[5pt] x_3(t) & = y'' \end{align}

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

\begin{align} y(2) &= x_1(2) = -1 \\[5pt] y'(2) & = x_2(2) = 1 \\[5pt] y''(2) & = x_3(2) = 2 \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) &= y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y'' \\[5pt] x_3'(t) & = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = -3y' . \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = -3x_2. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(2)= -1 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3, \quad& x_2(2)= 1 \\[5pt] x_3' = -3x_2, \quad& x_3(2)= 2 \end{cases} \]

Finally, $p=-1, q=1, r=2, f(t) = -3x_2,$ and

\begin{align*} (p+q-r)\cdot f(t) & = (-1+1-2)(-3x_2) \\[5pt] & = (-2)(-3x_2) \\[5pt] & = 6x_2. \end{align*}

question.text:
The third-order initial value problem \[ y''' - 6\sqrt{t}\,y'' + 12y' = 0 , \quad y(1)= -2, \quad y'(1)= 2, \quad y''(1)= -3 \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(1)= p \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3, \quad& x_2(1)= q \\[5pt] x_3' = f(t), \quad & x_3(1)= r \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t),$ $x_3(t) = y''(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate $(p+q-r)\cdot f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) &= y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'\\[5pt] x_3(t) & = y'' \end{align}

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

\begin{align} y(1) &= x_1(1) = -2 \\[5pt] y'(1) & = x_2(1) = 2 \\[5pt] y''(1) & = x_3(1) = -3 \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) &= y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y'' \\[5pt] x_3'(t) & = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = 6\sqrt{t}\,y'' - 12y' . \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = 6\sqrt{t}\,x_3 - 12x_2 . \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(1)= -2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3, \quad& x_2(1)= 2 \\[5pt] x_3' = - 12x_2 + 6\sqrt{t}\,x_3, \quad& x_3(1)= -3 \end{cases} \]

Finally, $p=-2, q=2, r=-3, f(t) = - 12x_2 + 6\sqrt{t}\,x_3,$ and

\begin{align*} (p+q-r)\cdot f(t) & = (-2 + 2 - (-3))(- 12x_2 + 6\sqrt{t}\,x_3) \\[5pt] & = (-2 + 2 + 3)( - 12x_2 + 6\sqrt{t}\,x_3) \\[5pt] & = 3(-6)( 2x_2 - \sqrt{t}\,x_3) \\[5pt] &= -18( 2x_2 - \sqrt{t}\,x_3). \end{align*}

question.text:
The third-order initial value problem \[ y''' + 3y'' - 4y' - 12y = 0 , \quad y(0)= 2, \quad y'(0)= 1, \quad y''(0)= 3 \] can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(0)= p \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3, \quad& x_2(0)= q \\[5pt] x_3' = f(t), \quad & x_3(0)= r \end{cases} \] where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t),$ $x_3(t) = y''(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate $(p-q+r)\cdot f(t).$
question.explanation:
First, we make the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1(t) &= y \\[5pt] x_2(t) & = y'\\[5pt] x_3(t) & = y'' \end{align}

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

\begin{align} y(0) &= x_1(0) = 2 \\[5pt] y'(0) & = x_2(0) = 1 \\[5pt] y''(0) & = x_3(0) = 3 \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1'(t) &= y' \\[5pt] x_2'(t) & = y'' \\[5pt] x_3'(t) & = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = -3y'' + 4y' + 12y. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = -3x_3 + 4x_2 + 12x_1. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \quad& x_1(0)= 2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3, \quad& x_2(0)= 1 \\[5pt] x_3' = 12x_1 + 4x_2 - 3x_3, \quad& x_3(0)= 3 \end{cases} \]

Finally, $p=2, q=1, r=3, f(t) = 12x_1 + 4x_2 - 3x_3,$ and

\begin{align*} (p-q+r)\cdot f(t) & = (2 - 1 + 3)(12x_1 + 4x_2 - 3x_3) \\[5pt] & = 4(12x_1 + 4x_2 - 3x_3). \end{align*}

question.text:
The third-order differential equation $y''' + 5y'' - 3t^2y'=0$ can be expressed as the matrix equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix}, \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & b \\ 0 & a & c \\ \end{bmatrix}, \] and for $y=y(t),$ we have \[ \begin{cases} y = x_1(t)\\[5pt] y' = x_2(t)\\[5pt] y'' = x_3(t). \end{cases} \]

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
question.explanation:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1 &= y \\[5pt] x_2 & = y'\\[5pt] x_3 & = y'' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1' = y' \\[5pt] x_2' = y''\\[5pt] x_3' = y''' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3,\\[5pt] x_3' = y'''. \end{cases} \]

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain \[ y''' = - 5y'' + 3t^2y'. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y''' = -5x_3 + 3t^2x_2. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = x_3 \\[5pt] x_3' = 3t^2x_2 - 5x_3 \end{cases} \]

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t)$ as follows: \[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1' \\ x_2' \\ x_3' \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 3t^2 & -5 \\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \\ x_3 \\ \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hence, $a=3t^2, b=1, c=-5,$ and $a+b+c = 3t^2 - 4.$

question.text:
The second-order differential equation $y'' + 3e^{2t}y' - 5y=0$ can be expressed as the matrix equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\end{bmatrix}, \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ c& d \end{bmatrix}, \qquad y(t) = x_1(t), \qquad y'(t) = x_2(t). \] Find the matrix $A.$
question.explanation:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1 &= y \\[5pt] x_2 & = y' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1' &= y' \\[5pt] x_2' & = y'' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = y''. \end{cases} \]

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain \[ y''= - 3e^{2t}y' + 5y. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = -3e^{2t}x_2 + 5x_1. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = 5 x_1 - 3e^{2t}x_2 \end{cases} \]

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t)$ as follows: \[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1' \\ x_2' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 5 & -3e^{2t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hence, $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 5 & -3e^{2t} \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text:
The second-order differential equation $3y'' + 9\sin{t}\,y' + y=0$ can be expressed as the matrix equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\end{bmatrix}, \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ c& d \end{bmatrix}, \qquad y(t) = x_1(t), \qquad y'(t) = x_2(t). \] Find the matrix $A.$
question.explanation:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1 &= y \\[5pt] x_2 & = y' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1' &= y' \\[5pt] x_2' & = y'' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = y''. \end{cases} \]

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain \[ y'' = -3\sin{t}\,y' - \dfrac{1}{3}y. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = -3\sin{t}\,x_2 - \dfrac{1}{3}x_1. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = -\dfrac{1}{3}x_1 - 3\sin{t}\,x_2 \end{cases} \]

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t)$ as follows: \[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1' \\ x_2' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -\dfrac{1}{3}& -3\sin{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hence, $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -\dfrac{1}{3}& -3\sin{t} \end{bmatrix}.$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

question.text:
The second-order differential equation $2y'' + y' - 3y=0$ can be expressed as the matrix equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\end{bmatrix}, \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ c& d \end{bmatrix}, \qquad y(t) = x_1(t), \qquad y'(t) = x_2(t). \] Find the matrix $A.$
question.explanation:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables: \begin{align} x_1 &= y \\[5pt] x_2 & = y' \end{align}

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get \begin{align} x_1' &= y' \\[5pt] x_2' & = y'' \end{align}

which we can rewrite as

\[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2, \\[5pt] x_2' = y''. \end{cases} \]

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain \[ y'' = - \dfrac{1}{2}y' + \dfrac{3}{2}y. \]

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives \[ y'' = -\dfrac{1}{2}x_2 + \dfrac{3}{2}x_1. \] Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: \[ \begin{cases} x_1' = x_2 \\[5pt] x_2' = \dfrac{3}{2} x_1 - \dfrac{1}{2}x_2 \end{cases} \]

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t)$ as follows: \[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1' \\ x_2' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ \dfrac{3}{2} & -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hence, $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ \dfrac{3}{2} & -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}.$
